Are other cultures critical of people for doctoring their hot beverages the way Americans are of people who don't drink coffee black?

What do you mean by "doctoring"? I'm not familiar with it in this context, but I'm going to assume you mean something akin to "changing how it should be drunk".

If Australia was to have a national hot beverage, it would likely have to be Milo (malt + chocolate drink). This of course differs from coffee - it's more akin to hot chocolate. Everybody drinks it the same way (mixed with milk or mixed with water, no other additives). Nobody would care if you drank it differently, but it just isn't done.

Most people over here drink coffee and tea as their regular hot daytime beverages. People drink coffee in dozens of different ways - drip brewing and similar is the latest hipster fad, but most people still drink espresso based coffees like caffè lattes, cappuccinos etc. There are also dozens of different types of teas, but the most common is black (akin to English Breakfast). Drinking tea black is slightly more of an Australian tradition, but in the bush a dash of milk would be added so that the flies could be picked out of the cup during summer.

I don't think that, culturally speaking, Americans care one way or the other. Sure, you'll find individuals who, for reasons I can't explain, see it as important to "fix" the way others drink coffee. But I don't see that as a cultural norm or more.

For full disclosure, I drink my coffee black, after passing the horseshoe test. That is, throw in a horseshoe. If it floats, the coffee's ready.

Materials Used For Bucket:

  • 5 x White 5gal Buckets (stackable)

  • 5 x CDL Daytime bulbs w/ highest lumen count you can find (@ 1600 lumens each = 8000 lumens total - Picture 4)

  • 2 x Two-way bulb-to-light-socket adapter (Seen in Picture 4)

  • 3 x 1-way bulb-to-power-socket adapter (Seen in Picture 4)

  • 1 x Humidity sensor w/ temperature readout

  • 2 x 80mm PC fans

  • 1 x 120mm PC fan

  • 1 x 1A power supply (Picture 6)

  • 1 x Mechanical light timer (Picture 6)

  • 1 x wire-to-plug adapter, for convenience (Picture 7)

  • 1 x SURGE-PROTECTED Power Strip

  • Over 9000 black duct tape

Growing Medium and Nutrients:

  • 1 x bag Fox Farms Happy Frog soil

  • 1 x bag Miracle-Gro Perlite

  • 1 x Fox Farms Nutrient 3-Pack: Grow Big, Big Bloom, Tiger Bloom (Picture 8, sans Tiger Bloom)

  • 1 x pH kit (Picture 8)

  • 1 x ppm meter (Picture 8)

  • 1 x fine mist spray bottle

  • 1 x Tsp measuring cup (I'm in the US, not sure if metric or imperial)

  • 1 x small bag of plant ties

  • 1 x planter's net for SCROG

The Bucket & Spacers

Pick out a bucket that will hold the plants, and wrap it entirely in black duct tape. If you couldn't find white 5gal buckets and got a different color, line the inside of the bucket with tin foil so the inside light will be reflected and not absorbed by the bucket walls. White buckets reflect the light just fine without the lining, but you can line white buckets if you really want to.

For the remaining buckets, cut the lids off, leaving about 2"-3" of plastic to it doesn't slip off somehow - I left 4"-5" because I was lazy and this is only crucial if the extra plastic will hit a fan or whatever else you have installed in the sides of the bucket. You can always cut more off, too.

NOTE: I installed my dedicated top exhaust fan between two spacers - it took a bit of work since I didn't have proper tools, but it was straightforward...make a space big enough for the fan, secure it facing outwards (exhaust), wire it up and test it.

Drainage

I have a soldering iron, but a drill/hammer+nail will work just fine...anything that makes a hole, really. Make a circular grid of holes in the bottom of the primary bucket, spaced out about 2-3 inches.

Lights

I was originally plugging the lights directly into the 1-way socket adapters, so they were sticking straight out from the power strip. This isn't the most efficient and I've since adopted an updated design to spread light more evenly. Plug the three 1-way adapters into the power strip, skipping a socket between each. Get the bucket lid and turn the power strip over so it's standing on those 1-way adapters, position the strip on the lid so the lights will be centered, and trace and cut out the area for each adapter on the lid. Push the adapters through and see if everything lines up and stays in place, adjusting where necessary. Once you're happy with the power strip's position, screw the two 2-way bulb-to-light-socket adapters into the 1-way adapters at each end of the strip, making sure the "Y" shape is perpendicular to the length of the power strip (sticks out to the sides). Screw the light bulbs to make sure the socket positioning is good and place the lid on your bucket, then plug in the power strip. If the bulbs are spaced evenly and everything looks good to you, set it aside.

Fans + Air Flow

NOTE: As you add spacers to keep the lights from burning the plant, more and more hot air will stay up towards where the lights are, and the 80mm fans towards the bottom of the bucket may not be able to get that air out. I added a 120mm PC fan up next to the lights as a dedicated exhaust, and my temps are just fine. This also helps lower humidity, which can lead to powdery mildew, which is no bueno.

Find where on the sides of the bucket you want your fans to go, ensuring the wires from each fan meet at some point on the outside of the bucket with a bit of slack, which is where the plug for power will be. I placed my fans about 6"-8" up from the bottom of the bucket on either side - one for intake, one for exhaust. NOTE: If you only have one fan available to you, use it for exhaust. Trace the fans on the bucket and cut out the plastic, then insert the fans making sure the direction of air flow is pointing the correct way. I didn't need to tape them in place because I was able to squeeze them through the hole, which was just a shade too small, so they're held in place pretty well. Take the fan wires, strip about 1/2" of plastic off the end, then join the two red ends together, and the black ends together. DO NOT CONNECT RED TO BLACK, OR VICE VERSA. Twist the metal wires together to form two wire ends, then get the adapter and put the red ends into the positive (+) slot and the black ends into the negative (-) slot. Use a screwdriver to fasten the ends into place...you may need to re-adjust if the ends slip out easily - I like to hold everything by the adapter so the fans dangle...if the wire ends slip out, re-adjust/re-tighten. Test the fans with the 1A power supply, and if both fans turn on and move a good amount of air, go ahead and mount them in the sides of the bucket, again making sure one is for intake and the other is for exhaust.

Extras

I added a watering apparatus to the side of my bucket, but this is completely optional...I'm just a dork. It consists of numerous PVC parts and feed water into the bucket through a plastic tube with holes in it. Decently effective, more for show than anything :)

I also mounted my humidity sensor in the side of the bucket, display facing out and the back entirely covered save for the actual sensor that needs access to air. I don't worry about accidentally watering it and I don't have to open my bucket for a reading.

I got a planter's net to have a SCROG, but the spacing between the threads is about 5"-6" wide. In Picture 5, the center 'X' is actually another piece of the net imposed over a big empty square, which is the actual net's size. For about 15 min of figuring out the best way to do this, I'm happy with it.

That plastic cup is another seed that I'm going to grow in a 12/12 cycle from the start, to compare yields. It hasn't sprouted in about 3 days, but I'm not too concerned - the vendor gave me 3 extra seeds as part of a promotion, so it isn't the end of the world if it doesn't make it :) I also think I mixed too much Perlite into the cup's soil, so I may try again with less next time if this one doesn't pan out.

The Soil & Nutrients

I put a small, 1/2" layer of Perlite on the bottom of the bucket to help with drainage, and then filled about 4"-5" more with soil. I made a mix of about 1/3 Perlite to 2/3 soil which drains pretty well.

I'm using a 1/2 gal milk carton to measure out the Fox Farm nutrients, as their measurements are all per gallon - just cut all the measurements in half. I was a dummy and used Big Bloom instead of Grow Big for the first 2 waterings, and that's where I think those yellow spots on the lower leaves came from. I saw my mistake, fixed it, and three waterings later those yellow spots are subsiding and the plant growth is easily noticeable. Lesson learned: READ THE INSTRUCTIONS CAREFULLY AND OFTEN.

I water every other day, or whenever I notice the top 1/2"-1" of soil is dry. I tend to water lightly to keep runoff to a minimum, so every other day is about right. Though your situation may be different, you'll be able to determine the ideal watering schedule once you figure out how long your soil mix retains water for, etc.

I have a spray bottle that I use to keep the seed moist, and the two plants cool. I'm only using regular water, but I've heard of others using nutrient mix in their spray bottles. I may switch once the seed sprouts.

Lighting Schedule & Temps

As I mentioned, I got my two plants from a guy off craigslist in Oregon, so I was able to start with an 18/6 schedule - 18 hours of light, 6 hours of dark. If you're starting from a seed, I believe 24/0 is good until it sprouts and enters the veg phase, then switch to 18/6 for the rest of the veg phase until it reaches the desired height/size. The mechanical light timer is good because it's dead simple to use and is reliable. It's bad because if you lose power it can get thrown off, which actually happened the other day here, but that'd most likely happen with any timer you got, so it's not a deal-breaker for me.

My understanding is that the ideal humidity range starts at ~50-60% for veg phase and drops by ~5% every week, but you should do your own research, I remember there being some debate about that.

Ideal temps are between 70F-85F at all times. It's worth mentioning that I leave my fans running all the time. They plug into the wall directly and not into the timer-driven power strip. Temps at night can drop to 60F, but so far I haven't had any problems...it may take a bit longer till harvest but I'm a patient guy.

Please let me know if you have any questions! I'll be updating this from time to time, so if you notice anything that seems out of place, or if I'm completely wrong regarding any of my information, please do not hesitate to correct me! I'd rather have the right info than be perfect the first time around :)
